summary: John's 5th-great-grandfather; Connecticut-born Pringle/Prindle who married Ensign Thomas Lamoreaux's daughter in Orange County, NY, and pioneered at Plymouth, PA, from the 1790s.
bio: Samuel Pringle (often written Prindle) was born about 1767 (tree 1767-1847; one online tree says c.1770; WikiTree gives Monroe, Orange Co., NY, c.1767 without a record; FamilySearch says born in Connecticut). The Harvey Book says Samuel and James Pringle, 'brothers (presumably natives of Connecticut)', lived several years in Orange County, NY, before 1790, that the name was often written Prindle, that 'several of the name of Pringle and Prindle' were among the original purchasers of New Milford, CT, in 1703, and that the family descended from a Scottish emigrant. Round 3 rates Newtown/New Milford, Fairfield Co., CT as the probable home area. In Orange County a sibling group - David (m. Susannah Lamoreux 1783), James (m. Phebe Lamoreux 1785), Samuel (m. Martha 1790) and Hannah (m. Isaac Lamoreux 1790) - married four Lamoreuxs. FamilySearch (G99D-9DZ -> L8MP-W4X) makes Samuel a son of James Prindle (b. Newtown CT 5 Aug 1736; m. 22 Jan 1759 'Anar' [Hannah] Turner; d. Newtown 9 Nov 1800) with children James (c1754), David (1757), Benjamin (1764), Samuel (c1767) and Hannah (1773); The Prindle Genealogy (1906, p.41) confirms that James Prindle but lists no children, so this remains speculative. Round 2's suggestion that Benjamin Prindle, private in the 1st Regt, Orange Co. militia, was his father is downgraded: Benjamin now looks like a brother. Samuel married Martha Lamoreaux, eldest daughter of Thomas and Keturah, in 1790 (FamilySearch: at Smith's Clove, Orange Co.; an HSP marriage record image could not be opened). The Harvey Book says both families moved to Plymouth in 1794 (Thomas Lamoreaux himself moved in spring 1790 - conflict). A 'Samuel Prindle' is in the 1800 Plymouth census; he is on the 1796 assessment list and was Supervisor of Roads in 1800. He built a stone farmhouse near what became the Gaylord coal shaft; by 1873 'heaps of culm and stacks of machinery' had defaced it, and if the old farmer's spirit returned 'it is very doubtful... whether he could recognize the locality' (Wright p.391). An early Plymouth store's account books list him among regular customers buying 'rum, whisky, tobacco and snuff' (Wright p.308). He died 25 Mar 1847 in Kingston Twp (WikiTree; Harvey: 'March 1847') and is buried in Shupp's Cemetery, Larksville (FamilySearch). The Harvey Book says he and Martha had five sons (eight children in all); five are identified: Thomas (1791-1861), Benjamin (1794-1853), James (c.1799), Temperance (c.1802) and probably Samuel Jr. (m. Huldah Ives); John (m. Phoebe Davenport) is speculative.
funFacts: His stone farmhouse was swallowed by culm heaps near the Gaylord shaft by 1873.
The store ledger shows his household's luxuries: rum, whisky, tobacco and snuff.
